query: Single-phase high-entropy alloys have difficulty achieving a satisfactory strength–ductility balance. Earlier work introduced the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure to enable large-sized production and obtain good strength and plasticity, but its performance still falls short of industrial requirements. Its use in aircraft and spacecraft fasteners further requires stability under extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosion, while relevant creep and corrosion studies remain limited by sample-size and experimental-environment constraints. Given these limitations and design requirements, what single intervention could improve the alloy’s practical performance? Present one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted improvement over the starting material, boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a feasible experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor, controlled amount of yttrium (Y) and hafnium (Hf) into the cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy will improve its high-temperature stability, room-temperature creep resistance, and corrosion resistance without a detrimental loss in the strength–ductility balance.
generation.material_initial_state: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy produced by conventional casting that exhibits a uniform fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure.
generation.intervention: Modify the alloy composition by incorporating minor amounts of Y and Hf during the casting process (i.e. a Y/Hf co-doping intervention), keeping the overall eutectic composition essentially unchanged.
generation.conditions: The doped HEA is processed using the same conventional casting route as the baseline alloy, with controlled Y/Hf additions at levels set by the dopant’s controlled variable. Mechanical and environmental evaluations are performed under conditions simulating aerospace fastener service—namely, tests under cyclic extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term static load (creep) at room temperature, and aggressive corrosion environments (e.g. molten salt or Na2SO4/NaCl exposure).
generation.structural_mediator: The Y/Hf additions are expected to promote the formation of stable, finely dispersible oxide or intermetallic particles at or near phase boundaries, which in turn retard grain boundary diffusion and coarsening.
generation.mechanism: By refining the microstructure and stabilizing the lamellar phase interfaces, the Y/Hf dopants reduce the mobility of grain boundaries and inhibit diffusion-based creep under long-term static loads. Simultaneously, their presence facilitates the formation of protective oxide scales that improve corrosion resistance. Together, these effects lead to improved overall operational stability without compromising the alloy’s balance of strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the undoped AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy, the Y/Hf-doped variant will exhibit lower creep rates, enhanced resistance to thermal fluctuation–induced degradation, and reduced corrosion damage while maintaining or even slightly improving its tensile strength and ductility.
generation.baseline: The as-cast, undoped AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy.
generation.boundary: The intervention is expected to be effective when the Y/Hf additions are kept at low levels that do not disrupt the eutectic lamellar microstructure; its performance is validated under aerospace-relevant thermal, mechanical, and corrosive testing conditions.
generation.uncertainty: The optimum concentration of Y and Hf and the detailed long-term stability improvements (quantitative creep rate reduction, corrosion spallation area reduction) require further empirical calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: (a) the baseline AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy and (b) a series of Y/Hf-doped alloys with controlled dopant levels. Subject both sets to identical processing conditions and then conduct a series of tests simulating service conditions—room-temperature creep tests under constant load, cyclic thermal fluctuation tests, and corrosion tests under aggressive salt environments.
measurements: Creep rate under static load at room temperature
Tensile strength and ductility via standard stress–strain tests
Extent of microstructural stability and phase integrity via SEM/TEM analysis
Corrosion performance via spallation area measurements or mass loss after exposure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Y/Hf-doped samples do not display a statistically significant improvement in creep resistance and corrosion performance, or if they suffer a degraded strength–ductility balance compared to the undoped alloy under identical test conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractBoth crack-free AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) and Y and Hf co-doping AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA (YHf-EHEA) coatings were prepared by laser cladding. The solidification microstructure, thermal stability, and hot corrosion performance of the coatings at 900 °C under 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl molten salts were investigated. The experimental results showed that the structure of the as-deposited coatings consisted of FCC and BCC/B2 phases. After heat treatment, an Al-rich L12 phase was precipitated in the FCC phase of all coatings. The grain sizes of the EHEA and YHf-EHEA coatings after heat treatment at 900 °C for 10 h increased by 27.5% and 15.7%, respectively, compared to the as-deposited coatings. Meanwhile, after hot corrosion, the spallation areas of the YHf-EHEA and EHEA coatings accounted for 14.98% and 5.67% of the total surface area, respectively.
